On the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken another step towards its long-standing vision of turning the iPhone into a single sheet of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving this without the Face ID components showing through the display or compromising screen quality in that area requires some remarkably clever engineering…

Jony Ive once described his long-term vision for the iPhone's design as a single piece of glass, and although he has left the company, that goal has endured. Apple ultimately wants to embed all the technology that currently occupies screen space — including Face ID and the front-facing camera — beneath the display.

The iPhone 18 Pro has become the first to deliver on the former, but it has been anything but easy. Face ID requires the TrueDepth module to both emit and receive infrared light, and infrared cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple had to create gaps between the pixels large enough for infrared light to pass through, without causing any visible degradation to the display. To achieve this, the company's engineers set about designing an entirely new pixel arrangement that widens the gaps without noticeably affecting what those pixels can display.

iFixit has showcased this pixel pattern under the microscope, and Apple confirmed to me that the overall pixel density across the entire module area has been halved. This could have created a second problem: halving the pixel density would likely make that area of the display noticeably dimmer, so Apple has boosted the brightness of these pixels to compensate. It also appears to have added an infrared filter that blocks visible light from passing through the gaps, further concealing the components.

The result is quite remarkable. In everyday use, the TrueDepth camera assembly is completely invisible even when looked at closely up close. I tried macro photography under various display colours and lighting conditions and was unable to capture it on camera. Of course, that doesn't mean it can't be detected at all — iFixit's microscope images show it clearly — but in daily use, you absolutely won't notice it.

This breakthrough currently allows the Dynamic Island to shrink in size, in turn supporting three Live Activities on display rather than just two. On some future iPhone model, the front-facing camera will also be hidden beneath the display. The technology is already feasible today, but the trade-offs in image quality remain beyond what Apple is willing to accept. It's only a matter of time before that gets resolved.
